entries.title: Amazon Kindle e-reader prices have increased
entries.summary: Amazon increased Kindle e-reader prices significantly due to rising memory and storage component costs. The post Amazon Kindle e-reader prices have increased first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon has recently raised prices on its Kindle e-readers across its main hardware lines. The entry-level and mid-range models, including the basic Kindle, Paperwhite, and Signature versions, now come with higher price tags than their predecessors. The only exception to this price hike is the Kindle Scribe, which was already on the pricier side.

The 16GB Kindle Paperwhite has seen a price jump to $199 for the ad-supported model, which is an increase from the previous $159. Meanwhile, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is now available for $249, reflecting a significant overnight hike of $50. In addition, the basic Kindle’s price has risen by $40. It’s currently priced at $149 with ads, and $169 without.

Industry observers connect these shifts to rising component and memory storage costs driven by broader hardware supply pressures. Social media is lamenting these price changes, but is saying that due to an upcoming sale in October, the prices might go back to the normal price for a limited time.

This is the first time that Amazon has increased e-reader prices in a very long time. Not only is this the new reality for USA customers and all of Amazon’s distribution partners such as Best Buy, but prices have risen internationally, in countries such as Canada and the United Kingdom.

Amazon is not the only company to change their pricing. Major manufacturer Kobo implemented price hikes ranging from $10 to $30 on all of their current-generation e-readers earlier this year.

entries.title: Digital Piracy and Malware: Why Downloading Free Content Can Put Your Devices at Risk
entries.summary: eBook piracy is costing US publishers close to $300 million a year, and that number keeps climbing as file-sharing websites and torrent trackers get much easier to stumble upon The post Digital Piracy and Malware: Why Downloading Free Content Can Put Your Devices at Risk first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
eBook piracy is costing US publishers close to $300 million a year, and that number keeps climbing as file-sharing websites and torrent trackers get much easier to stumble upon. Readers download compressed archives thinking they got it easy and that they’re getting a free copy of the latest bestseller, and in a lot of situations, they do get that. Yet, buried in that ZIP or RAR folder can be something else no one is aware of. Malware developers have figured out that pirated content is one of the easiest ways to get onto someone’s computer, because the person who downloads it already expects a slightly shady process. So, free isn’t really free, as it just moves the cost somewhere else.

How Pirated Content Hides Malware

The trick that occurs is almost always in the packaging. A pirated book rarely shows up as a single EPUB file. It comes wrapped in pirated eBooks malware, carrying a compressed file with other formats like MOBI and PDF, sometimes even an AZW3 for good measure, so the download looks legitimate and complete. Somewhere in there, though, there’s often an .exe file disguised as a reader application, a font package, or an “unlock tool” needed to open the book.

Run that file and the malware will definitely install itself without you knowing. Some versions scan for cryptocurrency wallets while others sit in the background logging clipboard activity or pulling down extra payloads from a remote server once they’re inside the device. This malware has gotten so sophisticated that it can delete its own traces after running, which makes it harder for antivirus software to catch after it happens.

Even cracked apps work the same way. Whether it says it’s a free version of paid software or a modded APK, the delivery method barely changes. It comes bundled with the real thing and counts on the user to skip past the warnings to get what they came for.

The Real Risks of Downloading Pirated Content

Once the malware is on the device, what it does differs. Some strains go after saved passwords and login sessions, taking in all the credentials from the browsers, while others are built to mine cryptocurrency in the background, using up processing power without the owner noticing until the fan doesn’t stop running. Clipboard hijackers are a newer favorite, where they wait until someone copies a crypto wallet address, then they swap it for the attacker’s own. Ransomware, however, is the blunt-force version that locks up files until a payment is made.

None of this is limited to Windows users, either. Mac users tend to assume they’re outside the blast radius because of Apple’s ecosystem and its reputation. However, that doesn’t hold up once cracked software enters the picture, as the risks of installing cracked apps on Mac are largely detrimental. Downloading pirated apps produces pirated apps security risks that are largely OS-agnostic, and the risks are close enough to what happens to any other device. That means treating one as a safer option is a mistake, as that doesn’t reflect the reality of the situation. A modified installer can request the same permissions a legitimate one would, and by the time anyone thinks twice about it, the software is already installed.

That simply means one shouldn’t neglect the risks, regardless of the device being used.

Why Pirated Apps Are Just as Dangerous as Pirated eBooks

eBooks aren’t the only thing getting people into trouble here. The same logic applies to any cracked software, modded APKs on an Android device, and anything advertised as a free version of a real program that normally costs some amount of money. Digital piracy and malware go hand in hand here, no matter what’s being downloaded, as the incentive for whoever’s distributing it is identical. They want to bury something profitable inside a file people already really want.

Modded APKs are especially common in app stores that don’t vet uploads the way Google and Apple do. Someone downloads what looks like a paid photo editor or a game with great features, and inside the installer exists a code that has nothing to do with photo editing. Downloading pirated content risks the user not knowing what’s happening for a long time, as people associate danger with sketchy torrent files, not app stores or even unofficial ones.

The FBI’s National Intellectual Property Rights Coordination Center has said plainly that illegally copied apps, including counterfeit products made to look real, carry a real chance of containing malware. That wasn’t specific to one platform or one type of file, but it applies to anything, including a cracked design program or a pirated novel.

How to Tell If a Download Is Safe

There’s no foolproof way to know if you’re subjecting your device to piracy malware risks before clicking, but a few things tend to give a bad download away. Here is how you can tell:

  • Anything inside the archive with a .exe extension when you were only expecting a book or an image file
  • File names padded with extra words like “reader” or “unlock”
  • Installers that ask for permissions way outside what the program should need
  • Sites with no real domain history, poor spelling, or ads that redirect
  • ZIP or RAR files that are password protected, as that’s often done to stop antivirus scanners from checking what’s inside the extraction

Conclusion

That $300 million number isn’t going to go anywhere, but neither is the malware riding the downloads. Every free copy of a book or content always comes with skipping the price tag but taking on the risk. For most people, that is invisible until it costs a lot, whether it’s the device slowing down or a password stops working somewhere. Free was never really free, so if it charges later, that usually means it charges much more.

Markus lives in San Francisco, California and is the video game and audio expert on Good e-Reader! He has a huge interest in new e-readers and tablets, and gaming.

entries.title: NASA is giving away a bunch of free e-books
entries.summary: Read and download free NASA e-Books on the agency’s history, aeronautics research, science missions, and the International Space Station. The post NASA is giving away a bunch of free e-books first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
NASA publishes a vast collection of free e-books covering aeronautics, space station science, history, and planetary exploration that anyone can download. These digital books are available to the public at no cost in formats like PDF, EPUB, and MOBI through the official NASA E-Books Directory.

Most of the free e-books are going to only appeal to people with very scientific backgrounds. The books include the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, which outlines the precise methods used to manage complex space systems. Read about the history of flight, supersonic research, and X-planes that paved the way for modern aviation. Learn about deep space discoveries, atmospheric science, and planetary missions, complete with high-resolution imagery. Enjoy stunning coffee-table-style books filled with breathtaking pictures of galaxies, nebulae, and deep space. Access comprehensive accounts of the agency’s evolution, including texts like Orders of Magnitude: A History of the NACA and NASA.

entries.title: Viwoods AiPaper and AiPaper Mini have received cloud sync
entries.summary: The Viwoods Cloud is a secure, native synchronization ecosystem for Viwoods AiPaper tablets that provides 10GB of free cloud storage. The post Viwoods AiPaper and AiPaper Mini have received cloud sync first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Viwoods is updating its e-notebook software to 3.15 and introducing the Viwoods Cloud. The Viwoods Cloud is a secure, native synchronization ecosystem for Viwoods AiPaper tablets that provides 10GB of free cloud storage to sync notes, reading progress, and documents across multiple devices. It acts as a bridge to manage files, though it operates alongside major third-party cloud platforms.

You can toggle automatic syncing independently for specific native applications like Paper, Meeting, Knowledge Base, Memo, and Daily. It automatically saves and syncs reading progress, bookmarks, highlights, and handwritten annotations for uploaded e-books. You can log in via cloud.viwoods.com on any web browser to preview notes, download documents, or upload files from a computer straight to the tablet.

Instead of forcing you into a proprietary cloud ecosystem, Viwoods integrates natively with major cloud storage providers. You can link your accounts to enable one-click, automatic synchronization to Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive, and Dropbox.

For users concerned with data privacy, Viwoods also includes ViTransfer. This is a local, peer-to-peer file transfer pipeline rather than a traditional cloud storage locker. It generates an encrypted temporary bridge between your tablet and a computer/phone where files auto-delete after 24 hours, ensuring no residual data is left on the web.

entries.title: Podcast: Amazon Kindle and AI Destruction of books
entries.summary: The Good e-Reader Radio show talks about the destruction of hardcover books by AI companies like Amazon. The post Podcast: Amazon Kindle and AI Destruction of books first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Today on the Good e-Reader Radio show, we talk about how AI companies are buying millions of physical books, including vintage, out-of-print, and hard-to-find titles—slicing off their spines with industrial cutting machines and scanning the loose pages to train large language models. This process, often called “destructive scanning,” has sparked severe cultural and ethical backlash from authors, historians, and booksellers.

If you have a Kindle Oasis, Amazon has just implemented new e-book encryption that makes backing up the books and breaking the DRM impossible. If you use Overdrive Libby to borrow e-books from the public library in the United States, it is now impossible to extend the loan period by putting your Kindle into Airplane Mode.

entries.title: AI Companies are buying hardcover books and destroying them
entries.summary: The biggest fear for people who want to see books preserved through the training process is that AI firms will callously pulp rare books that can never be replaced. The post AI Companies are buying hardcover books and destroying them first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
AI companies are buying millions of physical books, including vintage, out-of-print, and hard-to-find titles—slicing off their spines with industrial cutting machines and scanning the loose pages to train large language models. This process, often called “destructive scanning,” has sparked severe cultural and ethical backlash from authors, historians, and booksellers.

Tech companies like Anthropic and Amazon are purchasing and bulk-scanning physical books published before 2022 to acquire high-quality, human-authored text free of synthetic “AI slop.” They are doing this because training language models on structured, long-form human writing helps them maintain grammatical reasoning and coherent style. Purchasing physical books legally allows owners to digitize them under fair use, bypassing the legal risks of using pirated digital copies.

Bookshops contacted by the Guardian say they have been receiving orders from buyers in the US, Canada, continental Europe and the UK. The increase has been replicated around the world, with booksellers in the US, Australia and Europe also reporting unusual orders. Jim Shaughnessy, the owner of MW Books in Claregalway, Ireland, said his business had been receiving large, varied orders since May. “They are sporadic, presumably machine-driven and have little in terms of thematic currency; books on agricultural implements in 18th century Africa through to biographies of 1950s racing car drivers,” he said. “Personally, I don’t see we have the right to dictate what any customer does with their purchases, but it is more than curious to see what’s being selected.”

Some Australian vendors speculated that AI companies are buying titles from 3rd parties and not doing it directly. This includes a Canadian company called Zoom Books, which describes itself as a book recycler. The orders usually came through large secondhand marketplaces like Abebooks or Biblio, where inventory can range from cheap paperbacks to rare, expensive items. Titles include a 1970s manual on soil mechanics, bought alongside a 2010 book called Born to Thunder: Champions of New Zealand Cycling, a collection of Early Australian Poetry, and a local history of the Melbourne suburb of Hawthorn.

Amazon singled out for destructive book scaning

In a recent investigation by 404 Media, a bookseller had a hunch that an order for 1,000 books placed on Biblio, a marketplace that allows buyers to remain anonymous, was linked to an AI company. To uncover the truth, they decided to discreetly place an Apple AirTag inside one of the books.

The tracking led them to a sprawling Amazon warehouse in Nevada, where employees revealed that their primary responsibility is to detach the spines from incoming books. This process enables them to scan the pages, but unfortunately, it results in the destruction of the books.

“I work at VGT3 here in Vegas, and our main task is scanning books,” an Amazon employee shared on a forum for Amazon workers, as cited by 404 Media. “Some team members are assigned to cut the books, while others handle receiving and scanning the barcodes. We didn’t have targets before, but now we do, although it’s not really stressful.”

Not every rare book is worth a fortune, but booksellers say many still carry real historical or sentimental value, the kind of value AI companies “don’t care about,” one told 404 Media. “They just want the content as a bunch of words strung together.”

The allegations against Amazon highlight a potential broader issue regarding the use of books for training AI models. A recent report from The Washington Post revealed that Anthropic faced scrutiny for training its Claude AI model on millions of books, which were subsequently destroyed. This operation, known as Project Panama, involved the tech company investing tens of millions of dollars into acquiring these books. The situation came to light through a copyright lawsuit filed by authors, which resulted in a significant $1.5 billion settlement from Anthropic. Recently, a judge unsealed documents related to this case, as noted by The Washington Post.

entries.title: Amazon Kindle Oasis now has new book encryption system
entries.summary: Firmware version 5.18.2.1.1 for the Kindle Oasis introduces Amazon's updated and hardened DRM protection. The post Amazon Kindle Oasis now has new book encryption system first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
In early 2026, Amazon quietly updated its older e-readers using Kindle software 5.18.5 or higher. Any books you have purchased or are going to purchase are using a new encryption called the KFX-ZIP format. This is not compatible with the encryption broken by 3rd-party tools for popular software such as Calibre and the DeDRM plugin.

Within the past couple of days, Amazon has updated all models of the Kindle Oasis running software 5.18.2.1.1 to use the new encryption system. All Kindle models except the Kindle Voyage are the only brand of e-readers that use the new e-book encryption system.

If you own a Kindle Oasis, there is no change to how you read e-books or download new content.

KFX-ZIP is an e-book container format used by Amazon Kindle. It packages Kindle Format 10 (KFX) files and their metadata into a zipped folder. Recent Kindle device firmware and desktop app updates apply stricter encryption to these files, making standard personal backup and third-party format conversion via tools like Calibre difficult or blocked. The new KFX format is not all bad; it has advanced features like improved typography and page fidelity.

Before Amazon implemented the new DRM changes, Amazon used to download e-books as KFX files, which were easily backed up to a user’s computer via USB cable, and then had their encryption broken to load the books on other devices or to create a local backup of prior purchases. Calibre and other software were common tools to break the encryption.

entries.title: When is the Boox Picco coming out?
entries.summary: The Boox Picco is an upcoming ultra-compact, pocket-sized e-reader announced by BOOX as the first device in their new "Tile" product line. The post When is the Boox Picco coming out? first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Around a month ago, Onyx Boox announced the Picco e-reader that will likely be its most affordable one ever. The upcoming product is designed to compete against the startup Xteink, which currently markets the X4 Pro and X3, with a few new models waiting in the wings.

The BOOX Picco 3.97inch e-reader is currently being teased by Onyx Boox. It will feature a black-and-white e-paper display with E-Ink technology. Users will be able to read during the day or night via the front-lit display, and upgraded storage will be available via an SD card. There appear to be buttons on the promotional image for page turns; it is also heavily rumoured that this device is a part of a new Tile product line.

However, the Boox ecosystem is far more expansive than Xteink. As long as the Picco has access to the Google Play Store, users will be able to download the Kindle, Kobo, and Libby apps. That means any of the books you read on your Kindle can be accessed and synced on the Picco.

Boox stated it will launch at an “accessible price point,” though exact pricing and a formal release date were not specified in the initial announcement. However, a possible launch will be at IFA in Berlin from September 4th to the 8th; this is where most new devices that are coming out by the end of the year make their debut.

entries.title: Lenovo ThinkPlus A510 has an E-ink display
entries.summary: The Lenovo thinkplus A510 is a premium, 10.3-inch color E-Ink office tablet running Android 14 that features standalone 4G LTE connectivity, a 20 MP document-scanning camera, and an advanced 8-microphone matrix designed for professional meeting transcription and digital note-taking. The post Lenovo ThinkPlus A510 has an E-ink display first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The Lenovo ThinkPlus AI Smart E-ink Screen Office Notebook A510 is a premium, productivity-focused E-Ink tablet running Android 14. Tailored specifically for professional mobile office use and digital note-taking, it stands out with its rare color paper display and built-in AI assistant features.

The Lenovo ThinkPlus A510 is a highly specialized 10.3-inch color E-Ink tablet that successfully bridges the gap between a traditional digital notepad and a mobile office workstation. By utilizing a vibrant Kaleido 3 color screen, it delivers crisp 300 DPI text for reading alongside a functional 150 DPI color canvas that makes annotating PDFs, viewing charts, and sketching feel remarkably natural. There is a built-in dual-temperature comfort light with adjustable warm and cool tones for strain-free reading in dark environments.

The inclusion of Android 14 provides access to a broad ecosystem of productivity applications. At the same time, built-in 4G LTE connectivity ensures professionals can stay synced and work securely from anywhere without relying on public Wi-Fi networks. Where the device truly shines is its dedicated suite of hardware tailored for business meetings and document management. It features a sophisticated eight-microphone matrix paired with AI-driven noise reduction, enabling it to capture crystal-clear audio and transcribe meetings seamlessly in real time. Supplementing this is a high-resolution 20 MP rear camera engineered specifically for scanning physical documents directly into editable digital formats, alongside a wireless magnetic stylus that boasts 4,096 levels of pressure sensitivity for fluid, lag-free note-taking.

However, the ThinkPlus A510 demands a premium price tag that reflects its niche, enterprise-focused design rather than mainstream consumer appeal. While its massive 6,900 mAh battery ensures exceptional longevity compared to standard LCD tablets, users primarily looking for an e-reader may find the device heavier and more complex than necessary. Ultimately, it is a powerful, premium tool built for executives, researchers, and mobile professionals who require advanced meeting transcription, color markup capabilities, and standalone cellular connectivity in a single, eye-strain-free device.

If you purchase through global e-commerce export platforms (such as AliExpress, Giztop, or Good e-Reader), expect the price to baseline between $850 and $950 USD. This markup accounts for international shipping fees, export packaging, and seller margins.
